text: – Wait, let me tell you about my meeting with Bai Ganyo – Stoycho spoke up.
– Come on, tell us – we all cried out, because we know that Stoycho knows how to tell such c o m e d i e s.

– And that was in Vienna. I was sitting one morning in the café, at Mendl's, I had ordered tea and started to look through our Bulgarian newspapers. I was engrossed in a very interesting article, which explained the way in which the constitution could be quite a bit shaken, even completely dismantled, and yet remain   u n t o u c h e d...   I was reading like that, carried away; at one point someone shouted in my ear: “O-o-oh! Good day!” – and a sweaty hand grabbed my right hand. I raised my eyes: a broad-shouldered, dark-eyed, dark-haired, and even dark-skinned gentleman, with twisted mustaches, with a high-cheekboned face, with a shaven but stubbly beard, dressed (in what do you think?) in a frock coat, unbuttoned, under his waistcoat a red sash two or three fingers wide, with a white (white in our fashion) shirt, without a tie, with a black, tilted kalpak, with boots and a Vratsa cane under his arm. A young man: he might be, he might be thirty years old at most.
– Excuse me, sir – I say to him with humble astonishment, – I do not have the pleasure of knowing you.
– What? Don't you recognize me, you say? You're Bulgarian, aren't you?
– I am Bulgarian.
– Eh?
– Eh?
– Come on, get up, let's go for a walk. Why are you just sitting around here? They call me Ganyo. Get up!
He didn't need to tell me he was Ganyo.
– Excuse me, Mr. Ganyo, I am not free now.
– Well, why are you sitting in the café if you're not free?
I did not deem it necessary to give him any explanations. But he showed not the slightest desire to leave me alone and suddenly blurted out:
– Get up and take me to the bathhouse. Where is the bathhouse here?

O-ho! To take him to the bath! I was starting to get a bit annoyed, but I restrained myself, and not only did I restrain myself, but I also felt like laughing. It was obvious that Bay Ganyo really needed a bath: he smelled sour from a distance. There was nothing to be done. A fellow countryman – I must serve him. And I thought to myself, I’ll take advantage of the occasion too, I’ll take a shower. It was hot. We set off and headed towards a summer bathhouse with a wide pool. Along the way, whenever we encountered something more remarkable, I always felt it necessary to point it out and explain it to Bay Ganyo, but I noticed that he listened to me reluctantly and would just let out an indifferent “Ah, is that so?” or “I know that” every now and then, with which, it seemed, he wanted to show me that he wasn't simple. Or he would interrupt me with some question completely irrelevant to what I was explaining. For example, I’m telling him something about the monument of Maria Theresa on the square between the Museums, and he pulls me by the sleeve.

– Look, that one over there, in the blue dress, eh? What do you think of her? Hey, tell me, how do you tell which one is that kind and which isn't? I’ve been mistaken many times, eh? – Bay Ganyo supplemented his question with a devilish wink.

We arrived at the bathhouse. My heart was tightening – it was as if it foreboded what was about to happen. We get our tickets at the counter. Bay Ganyo asks for "change" with a wiggling of his fingers, thrust into the window. The cashier hands him the remainder with a smile; Bay Ganyo fixes her with oily eyes, takes the money, and expresses his feelings with a peculiar cough. She bursts into laughter; Bay Ganyo, delighted, twirls his left mustache and shakes his head:
– How beautiful you are, madam. Hey, Stoycho, ask her if she knows Vlach. – Do you know Romanian? – Bay Ganyo himself asks.

At that time another visitor entered and we slipped into the common hall. A circular corridor. Around it were small dressing rooms, concealed by curtains. In the middle, a pool, separated from the corridor by a low wooden railing. One descends into the pool by several small stairs. Bay Ganyo and I took two adjacent rooms. I undressed quickly and entered the cool pool. In the water, several Germans were dutifully and silently stretching their muscles and puffing. Bay Ganyo lingered for a long time, and from behind the curtain of his room, groans were heard and some glass objects clattered; finally, the curtain was pulled back and he appeared in the flesh, with a hairy chest and legs patterned by his socks – holding a bundle in his hand: these were the precious vials, tied in a not-so-clean handkerchief, which he had been afraid to leave in the room. "How do you know their walls are sturdy? They'll pry off some board, and then go try to find them." He looked around the walls of the corridor, searching for a nail to hang his bundle on; he thinks that if it's a wall, there must be a nail on it, and turns to me:
– Such simpletons, these Germans; they haven't even got the sense to drive in a single nail, yet they say that we are the simple ones.

Having finally convinced himself of the stupidity of the Germans, Bay Ganyo hesitantly placed his handkerchief with the vials in front of the entrance to his little room, so that they would be before his eyes until he finished bathing.

– Listen here, boy – he turned to me, – you keep bathing, but keep an eye on the vials, and watch me, see what a stunt I'm going to pull off. – And with those words, Bay Ganyo lifted one of his legs and stepped onto the railing... – You just watch...

He raised himself, put his other leg in too, stood up, crossed himself and shouted:
– Look... Come on, God, help me... Hop!... – and threw himself into the air, curled his legs like a pretzel and splash! into the middle of the pool. Sheets of water sprayed upwards and showered over the heads of the Germans, frozen in astonishment; wavy circles bounced from the center to the edges, overflowed the pool, sank back again, and when the water settled and cleared after a few seconds, everyone present in the bath could see the hilarious gesticulations of Bay Ganyo under the water. He rose up, lowered his legs, stepped on the bottom, stood up with closed eyes and plugged ears, shook himself from the water – poof! – and sprayed water through his drooping mustache – poof! – and squeezed the water from his hair and face, opened his eyes, looked at me and laughed:
– Ha, ha, ha... eh? What do you say?...

I didn't manage to say anything, because he threw himself horizontally over the water and began slapping the surface with his hands, he began to swim "boatman-style": splash! – with his hand and he'd kick two kicks back, splash! with the other hand and two more kicks. The whole pool began to boil. As if we were under some waterfall. Waves splashed toward the edges, chains of droplets sprayed all the way to the opposite walls.
– This is what they call "the boatman way" – shouted the triumphant Bay Ganyo through the waves; – wait now, let's show them what they call a "vampor".

And turning onto his back, he began to deal such merciless blows with his feet upon the surface of the foamy water that splashes flew as high as the ceiling. He rapidly rotated his arms to represent the wheel of a steamship: "Tupa-lupa, tupa-lupa, fyuuuu," and Bay Ganyo whistled with his mouth.

The Germans froze in their tracks. They, in all likelihood, took my companion for some newcomer, an Oriental not yet committed to a madhouse, and I noticed on their faces not so much indignation as pity. But Bay Ganyo, it seems, read on their faces boundless amazement at his prowess, and so he quickly climbed the stairs, stood a bit wide-legged, looked haughtily at the Germans, began to strike his hairy chest heroically, and cried out victoriously:
– Bulgar! Bulga-ar! – and struck his chest even harder.

The proud tone with which he uttered this recommendation spoke volumes; this tone said: “Here he is, do you see him, the Bulgarian! This is he, that’s what he’s like! You have only heard of him, the hero of Slivnitsa, the Balkan genius! Here he is now before you, in his entirety, from head to toe, in the flesh! Do you see what wonders he is capable of performing! And is that all! Oho, what other things he is capable of! The Bulgarians were simple, were they! You rascals, you kikes!”
– Hey, ask if there’s any soap – said Bay Ganyo to me, after his patriotic enthusiasm had cooled down a bit, – look at what my feet have come to look like...

And indeed, his legs were not the most suitable model for the Apollo Belvedere. The patterns of his socks had imprinted themselves on the skin—already dirty and hairy. Moreover, we cannot surprise the Bulgarians with filth: we cannot make even the most vivid imagination conceive of something filthier than what reality itself can present to you...
With these words, Stoycho finished his story.
